paras: The threatened lynching of R. B. Williams occurred in Larned, Kansas, on the evening of August 1, 1903, after Williams, a Black tailor, shot and killed Clyde Langdon, a young white man, in his shop during a dispute over a suit of clothes. A mob formed with talk of lynching him, but officers took Williams by train to Hutchinson before any attack. A coroner's jury found that he had fired in self-defense, and by his own account he was released at his preliminary hearing.

Williams kept a tailor shop in the city building at Larned, and a Hutchinson dispatch called him "the negro preacher and tailor." Langdon, about 28 according to the Barton County Democrat, had come from Topeka and worked at a Larned restaurant.

Langdon had left a suit with Williams to be pressed, and according to the first Larned dispatch he found it not ready on Saturday evening and insisted it be returned at once. Inquest testimony gave a fuller sequence: after several visits that day about clothes he had partly paid for, Langdon came with a pistol, demanded his money back and pointed the weapon at Williams. Williams took up a pistol hidden under cloth on his work table and fired until, in his words, his gun was empty; Langdon died within minutes. Williams then called the city marshal, handed over both guns and gave himself up.

Within minutes of his jailing a mob formed, "with the avowed intention of lynching the murderer," as the Barton County Democrat put it. The marshal, a deputy and Sheriff McCoy told Williams they were taking him away "for your good," drove him by buggy to the junction east of town and put him on an east-bound Santa Fe train. He was lodged in the Reno County jail at Hutchinson at midnight.

Williams was brought back to Larned on Monday, August 3, and a large crowd followed him to the jail, but the Topeka State Journal reported "no demonstration." On the testimony of three witnesses the coroner's jury found self-defense, which the Barton County Democrat summed up as Langdon "hunting trouble" and making "the first gun play." According to Williams, at his preliminary hearing on Tuesday the court refused to bind him over, judged him "guilty of no crime" and ordered him set at liberty. No report mentions any arrest of members of the mob.

The first wire report ran on August 2 from Wichita to Savannah, Cheyenne and Phoenix under headlines on the averted lynching, such as "Kansas Mob Too Late to Catch Negro" and "Escaped Lynching." The fuller Larned dispatch in the Topeka State Journal and the Abilene Weekly Reflector called the shooting "a sensational murder" and said Williams "whipped out a revolver." After the inquest the Wichita Daily Eagle headed its report "Shot in Self Defense," and a state news digest credited the officers under "Officers Prevented a Lynching."

Among Black papers, the Professional World printed the wire text under "Negro Tailor Is Murdered," though it reported that the tailor had done the killing, and later added an unsourced claim that Williams had been dismissed from a Missouri Methodist conference "for immoral conduct." The Wichita Searchlight noted that the tailor was a preacher and that the coroner's jury had found self-defense. The Topeka Plaindealer took his side, calling the killing a case of "a young white plugugly" who thought he could "bluff the Negro" as in Mississippi, and on August 21 printed Williams's letter under "It Was One of Those Cases of Kill or Get Killed." His discharge at the preliminary hearing appears only in that letter.

The early Larned dispatch said Williams drew first, while Williams's statement at Hutchinson, the sworn inquest testimony of three witnesses and his letter said Langdon pointed a pistol at him first. The wire story said the mob went to the jail and found Williams gone, but the Larned and Wichita reports said he was removed before any demonstration, amid "much talk of raising a mob." The Professional World's August 5 dateline conflicts with the August 1 date of reports already in print on August 2.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of R. B. Williams
bases: A crowd formed at Larned with the stated aim of lynching Williams after he shot Langdon, and officers removed him from the jail to prevent it; no one was harmed by the crowd (A2, A6, A15, A16).

A mob formed or talked of lynching Williams for killing Langdon (A2, A6, A15), but officers took him to Hutchinson before any attack and he was returned unharmed and released (A10, A12, A25); no one was killed by the crowd, so this was a threatened lynching, not a lynching.

The wire report, an independent Larned dispatch, the Great Bend weekly, a Hutchinson dispatch and Williams's own letter agree on the shooting, the lynching talk and the removal to Hutchinson (A2, A6, A7, A15, A24).

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: Williams shot Langdon after a quarrel over a suit; a mob went to the jail to lynch him but the sheriff had already taken him away by train.

accounts.label: Larned correspondent
accounts.gist: Langdon demanded his unready clothes and Williams 'whipped out a revolver' and fired, twice after Langdon fell; a mob formed with talk of lynching but the sheriff removed the prisoner before any demonstration.

accounts.label: Williams at Hutchinson
accounts.gist: Williams said Langdon had a gun leveled at him when he fired and that three witnesses would support him.

accounts.label: Coroner's jury
accounts.gist: Three witnesses said Langdon came with a revolver demanding money he had advanced and pointed it at Williams, who then fired; the jury found self-defense.

accounts.label: Williams's letter
accounts.gist: He tried to knock the revolver from Langdon's hand, fired until his gun was empty, surrendered to the marshal, was taken away by officers 'for your good', and was released at his preliminary hearing.

framing.detail: The first wire story ran under headlines on the averted lynching: 'Sheriff Prevents Threatened Lynching by Quick Work', 'Kansas Mob Too Late to Catch Negro', 'Escaped Lynching'.
The Larned dispatch called the shooting 'a sensational murder' and Williams a 'negro murderer', then the Wichita Daily Eagle reported him 'Justified for His Shooting' after the inquest.
Kansas digest items credited officers: 'Officers Prevented a Lynching.'
The Professional World ran the wire text under 'Negro Tailor Is Murdered' and later added an unsourced charge of 'immoral conduct' against Williams.
The Topeka Plaindealer cast Langdon as a 'young white plugugly' acting as if 'in mississippi' and printed Williams's account as 'Kill or Get Killed'.
